analysis.one_liner: Eases the proof workers need to win employment discrimination lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill never left its House committee and received no vote before the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the Civil Rights Act of 1964 so that a worker who shows an employer treated them differently, and then shows the employer's stated reasons are untrue and a pretext for discrimination, would win their case. Today courts use a more complicated burden-shifting test. The bill was introduced in July 1993, referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, sent to a subcommittee, and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who sue over race, sex, or other employment discrimination would face a clearer, lower evidentiary path: once they show a prima facie case and prove the employer's stated reasons are pretext, the practice would be established as unlawful. The bill spells out the rule in the statute, reducing dependence on shifting court doctrines.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes disparate-treatment discrimination 'established' when the worker proves a prima facie case by a preponderance of the evidence and shows either that the employer offers no rebuttal or that each stated nondiscriminatory reason is not true but a pretext for discrimination.
It clarifies this is not the only way an unlawful practice can be proven, so other paths to proof remain open.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would bear the cost of an easier-to-satisfy proof standard: more discrimination suits would survive, and employers would have to defend decisions where the stated business reason is shown to be untrue, even if other evidence is mixed.

drawbacks.text: Allowing a showing of pretext alone to establish discrimination would lower the evidentiary bar below current court practice, exposing employers to liability based on weaker records of proof and inviting more litigation over hiring, firing, and promotion decisions.

The bill was narrow and its sponsor had limited support: 27 cosponsors and no committee action suggest little appetite in the House to change the evidentiary framework so soon after the 1991 Civil Rights Act had already reworked parts of Title VII.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but targeted: clearer rules for workers proving intentional discrimination. The cost is a heavier litigation burden on employers and the possibility of more close-call suits succeeding. It is a genuine trade-off in employment-law design, not a giveaway in either direction.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, then to a subcommittee, and sat there until the 103rd Congress ended with no hearing, no vote, and no Senate companion action.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 28, 1993, by Rep. David Mann of Ohio.
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the day it was introduced.
On August 11, 1993, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Select Education and Civil Rights, and no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress.
The 103rd Congress ended January 3, 1995, so the bill died without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers facing discrimination claims are better off: the burden of proof workers must meet stayed as the courts had set it, and no new statutory standard made pretext alone enough to win.

for.name: Rep. David Mann
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to write a clearer, lower evidentiary standard for disparate-treatment discrimination claims into Title VII.

for.name: 27 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; 26 Democrats and 1 Independent signed on.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 28, 1993, and never scheduled action on it.

against.name: Subcommittee on Select Education and Civil Rights
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on August 11, 1993, and took no further action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 27 cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent; no Republican support appears in the record, and the Democratic-controlled committee never acted.

industries.note: An easier proof standard would mean more successful discrimination suits and higher litigation exposure. Their gain from the bill dying is that workers must still meet the more demanding court-established test.

industries.industry: Employment defense bar and HR compliance services
industries.note: The bill would simplify proof rules, reducing the value of complex burden-shifting defense strategies. It died, so the existing legal framework remains.
